analysis.title: US Equities: AI confidence is fading
key_insights: Client sentiment on the AI theme is about as negative as it has been in a long time, and the pessimism now shows in positioning and valuations.

GS prime brokerage data shows Tech was by far the most net sold sector globally for another week. The US Info Tech long/short ratio fell to its lowest level in the PB dataset, which goes back to 2016.

Flows have shifted from mainly long liquidation and de-grossing to a more pronounced pickup in new shorts. The GS cash desk saw persistent NVDA supply from long-only investors, with money rotating into hyperscalers and other large cap tech.
NDX snapped a four-week losing streak, helped by semis, but appetite to re-engage remains limited.

CTAs have been aggressively selling Tech, and CTA positioning in NDX is back near max short levels. With positioning this light, it probably does not take much positive news to spark a squeeze higher.

Semis have underperformed the S&P by more than 30 percentage points since June, the sharpest relative drawdown since 2002 but still short of the 1990s extremes. GS Research argues much of the move has gone too far, with some stocks discounting close to zero earnings growth in 2028.

The GS AI Semis basket (GSCBSMHX) trades at 11x 2028 earnings versus nearly 16x for the S&P, while consensus expects 31% earnings growth in 2028. At the S&P multiple, current prices would imply a ~6% earnings decline.

Two main investor concerns are who pays for the additional hundreds of billions of dollars of AI spending, and whether enough data centers can be built. The data center concern has grown since the elections, with questions about restrictions on new construction in states like Texas.

GS Research estimates that even in a bearish scenario, new data center capacity coming online in 2028 should be roughly in line with 2027 because of construction already underway. If additional projects proceed, the figure could be more than 50% higher. The question is how much growth slows, not whether the buildout stops.

Financing is the bigger worry. AI companies want to spend more than the cash they generate, so they must keep borrowing or raising outside capital, while borrowing costs are rising and investors question the payoff. GIR thinks existing NVDA commitments should hold but new deals of the same size may be harder to arrange. Credit markets already show higher borrowing costs.
NVDA earnings next week and a major equity capital markets event are flagged as possible catalysts for risk appetite. NVDA is down 30% and has fallen six weeks in a row.

The GS 2027 Markets Outlook expects AI spending to keep growing but the pace to possibly peak early next year. AI has driven corporate earnings and equity gains much more than the broader economy, so a spending slowdown could hurt stocks more than GDP.

Coppersmith thinks equities can grind higher after the positioning reset but prefers to be more selective. He would use weakness in parts of AI to add rather than chase rallies, expects more rotation beyond infrastructure into next year, and would stay disciplined on hedges.
